issues.description: The manuscript states that self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression and that all confidence intervals included zero, yet the Results report a statistically significant meta-analytic effect with an interval reported as excluding zero. This contradiction changes whether the replication supports a null effect or a small positive association.
issues.quote: Self-esteem did not relate to perceived opportunities for self-expression (across the seven replications, all 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for effect sizes included zero).

issues.description: The Results report the meta-analytic effect for connection as p = .065, but the Discussion describes it as significantly different from zero. This is a direct statistical interpretation error and affects the central conclusion about whether the original connection finding replicated.
issues.quote: However, the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero.

issues.description: The manuscript reports different fail-safe numbers for the same outcomes in different sections. For self-expression the Results say FSN = 3 but the Discussion says five; for connection the Results say FSN = 5 but the Discussion says 11. These inconsistencies undermine confidence in the reported computations and interpretation of robustness.
issues.quote: The FSN was 3 studies.

issues.description: The reported prediction intervals differ across sections. For self-disclosure safety, the Results report a 95% PI of [-.54, -.03], whereas the Discussion reports [-.40, -.15], apparently confusing the confidence interval with the prediction interval. This affects claims about expected effects in future studies.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was -.28, 95% CI [-.40, -.15], 95% PI [-.54, -.03], p < .001.

issues.subcategory: overinterpretation of confidence and prediction intervals
issues.description: The manuscript states that the CI and PI indicated future studies would show an effect between .01 and .14. A confidence interval estimates uncertainty in the mean effect, not the range of future study effects, and even a prediction interval is probabilistic and highly uncertain with only seven studies. The wording overstates the precision and certainty of prediction.
issues.quote: the 95% CI and prediction interval (PI) indicated future studies would show an effect size between .01 and .14

issues.description: The manuscript infers publication bias in the original study from smaller replication effects and prediction intervals. A smaller original-versus-replication estimate is compatible with publication bias, but also with sampling error, temporal changes in Facebook use, procedural differences, population differences, measurement differences, or regression to the mean. The design cannot identify publication bias in a single original study.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study.

issues.description: The manuscript claims that p-values between .04 and .05 are relatively more likely under the true null than under a false null. This is an overgeneralized and context-dependent statement; the evidential meaning of a p-value depends on power, prior odds, selection, and analytic practices. It is not a valid basis for discounting the original p = .05 result without further modeling.
issues.quote: p-values between .04 and .05 have been demonstrated to be relatively more likely in the case of a true null hypothesis than a false one

issues.subcategory: inconsistent original effect size for advantageous disclosure
issues.description: The original advantageous self-disclosure effect is reported inconsistently as -.30 and -.33. Table 1 gives beta = -.300, the abstract gives original effect size = -.30, while Table 3 and the Discussion use original r = -.33. This inconsistency matters because the manuscript compares replication effect sizes against the original effect.
issues.quote: Self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)

issues.subcategory: ambiguous and potentially reversed effect-size difference sign
issues.description: Table 3 labels the comparison as replication versus original, but the reported difference values appear to be original minus replication. The direction is not defined clearly, and textual interpretations such as replication effects being smaller can be confusing when effects differ in sign. This can lead readers to misinterpret which study produced the larger effect.

issues.subcategory: fail-safe number applied to nonsignificant meta-analysis
issues.description: The manuscript reports a fail-safe number for the connection outcome even though the meta-analytic effect is nonsignificant. Fail-safe N is intended to ask how many null studies would be needed to reduce a significant result to nonsignificance; applying it to a nonsignificant effect is not meaningful in the stated framework.
issues.quote: The point-estimate of the meta-analytic effect size was .09, 95% CI [-.01, .18], 95% PI [-.09, .26], p = .065. ... The FSN was 5 studies.

issues.description: The study tests four primary outcomes across seven individual replications, four meta-analytic effects, multiple effect-size-difference tests, and heterogeneity tests, but does not describe any multiplicity control or clearly distinguish confirmatory from exploratory inference. This is especially relevant for the self-expression meta-analysis, where p = .021 would not survive many common corrections across four outcomes.
issues.quote: For each of the four outcome variables, we present the standardized beta and p-value for the regressions.

issues.subcategory: sample size based on original N rather than power or precision
issues.description: The minimum replication sample size was set to the original study size of 80 rather than to an a priori power or precision target. Because the effects under study are small to moderate, individual replications with N around 80–90 are underpowered to detect or compare effect sizes precisely, leading to wide CIs and unstable site-level conclusions.
issues.quote: The CREP team specified the minimum sample size required for the replication; this size was generally set at the original study’s sample size ... 80 for the present study as this was the sample size in the original study

issues.subcategory: unaccounted study-level attrition from OSF forks
issues.description: The OSF project had 17 forks, but only seven studies were included. The manuscript does not account for the other ten forks, whether any collected data, why they failed to meet criteria, or whether unavailable results could bias the meta-analysis. This is a study-level attrition and selection problem.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 “forks” representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process ... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository.

issues.description: The meta-analysis included only studies that met the minimum sample size and posted data/results. Without a prospective meta-analysis protocol or accounting for incomplete projects, inclusion may depend on researcher decisions after initiation, introducing analytic flexibility and possible availability bias.
issues.quote: All seven studies were included in this meta-analysis.

issues.description: The authors explicitly state that missing-data procedures are unknown for some studies. Without knowing whether missing responses were listwise deleted, pairwise deleted, imputed, averaged with partial scale data, or otherwise handled, the analyses are difficult to evaluate or replicate and may not be comparable across sites.
issues.quote: Contributors did not always post analysis scripts, so procedures to account for missing data are not known for all studies.

issues.description: The manuscript indicates that scale scoring was not fully documented and that at least one study likely summed items while others mean-averaged them. Although linear transformations do not affect correlations, inconsistent scoring complicates descriptive comparisons, missing-data handling, and reproducibility.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study’s mean implied items were summed.

issues.description: The manuscript reports excluding five non-Facebook users but does not provide site-specific counts, denominators before exclusion, whether this exclusion was preregistered, how Facebook-user status was defined, or whether there were other exclusions. This limits reproducibility and assessment of selection bias.
issues.quote: Five participants who were not Facebook users were excluded from analyses.

issues.description: The replication studies varied in whether questionnaires were administered online, individually in the lab, or in groups. These modes can affect privacy, social desirability, attention, and responses about self-esteem and disclosure. The manuscript does not control for or test mode effects.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods). Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.description: Several studies altered Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale wording, item order, and response scale length. These deviations may change the measured distribution and interpretation of self-esteem, compromising strict direct replication and cross-site comparability.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items ... and (b) most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.description: Most studies did not collect race or other demographic variables, preventing assessment of sample comparability, demographic moderation, and generalizability. The justification that the original study did not report demographics is insufficient for a multi-site replication intended to assess robustness.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected because the original Forest and Wood (2012) research did not indicate any other demographic information was collected

issues.description: The samples were undergraduate students from five U.S. institutions, yet the manuscript frames the importance around billions of Facebook users and later makes broad claims about individuals with low self-esteem. The limited age, education, country, and platform-use context constrain generalizability.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.subcategory: nonindependence of studies from repeated institutions
issues.description: The meta-analysis treats seven study estimates as independent, but two samples came from BYU and two from IIT, likely sharing institutional population characteristics, procedures, and faculty/research-team influences. A model accounting for nesting by institution or sensitivity analyses would be more appropriate.
issues.quote: These CREP research teams represented five diverse institutions

issues.subcategory: limited validity evidence for Facebook perception measures
issues.description: The Facebook outcomes were measured with scales created by the original researchers, but the manuscript reports only item counts and internal consistency. It does not provide evidence that these scales validly measure self-expression, connection, safety, or advantageous disclosure across changing Facebook contexts and samples.
issues.quote: Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012).

issues.subcategory: perceptions treated as actual benefits or behavior
issues.description: The study measures participants’ perceptions of Facebook as safe, advantageous, expressive, or connecting, not actual disclosure behavior, actual social connection, or actual psychosocial benefits. Some conclusions and implications slide from perceived affordances to real benefits or behavioral tendencies.
issues.quote: All items were rated on a scale ranging from 1 to 7 with higher scores representing greater perceived expression, connection, safety, and advantages.

issues.description: The design is cross-sectional and based on self-reported self-esteem and self-reported Facebook perceptions collected in the same session. Associations could reflect unmeasured confounders such as gender, age, race, Facebook intensity, social anxiety, depression, social support, or platform preference. Causal or directional language should be limited.
issues.quote: After informed consent, participants completed the 10-item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale ... Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions

issues.subcategory: social compensation theory not directly tested
issues.description: The manuscript claims support for social compensation theory, but the studies did not measure the proposed mechanism, such as face-to-face anxiety, online anxiety reduction, compensation motives, or actual online social behavior. The available evidence supports only perceived safety/advantages, not the theory’s mechanism.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory ... However, the CREP studies did not include a measure of FTF vs. online anxiety

issues.description: The original and replication studies occurred in different social media ecosystems. The manuscript itself notes that participants in 2016–2017 may have implicitly compared Facebook to Snapchat or Instagram, whereas the original participants likely did not. This threatens the assumption that the replications measured the same construct under comparable conditions.
issues.quote: Participants in our replication studies may have been implicitly comparing Facebook usage to Snapchat and Instagram when rating its usefulness for self-expression and connection with others, whereas these platforms would not have been a consideration for participants in Forest and Wood’s (2012) study.

issues.description: The author note states that individual studies preregistered data collection and analyses, but it is unclear whether the meta-analysis inclusion criteria, effect-size extraction, handling of missing study information, moderator decisions, fail-safe analyses, and interpretation rules were themselves preregistered. This leaves researcher degrees of freedom at the synthesis stage.
issues.quote: the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study’s OSF page

issues.description: The manuscript gives a high-level description of using metafor but does not fully specify the exact effect-size variance calculations, whether Fisher z values or raw r values were supplied, whether Knapp-Hartung or normal inference was used, or how CIs/PIs were computed. Reliance on OSF syntax helps but the manuscript itself is incomplete for evaluating the analyses.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using the R package metafor (Viechtbauer, 2010). The rma function was used, which accepts the effect size r and N parameters

issues.subcategory: overreliance on heterogeneity tests with small k
issues.description: The Results interpret nonsignificant Q tests and low I2 estimates as little or no heterogeneity, but with only seven studies these tests are underpowered and variance estimates are unstable. Although the Limitations later acknowledge this, the Results still use language that may overstate homogeneity.
issues.quote: The between-study variance in the replication studies did not appear to be heterogenous, Q(df = 6) = 4.75, p = .576; T2 = 0, 95% CI [0, .03]; I2 = 0%, 95% CI [0%, 79%].

issues.subcategory: missing descriptive statistics table in manuscript text
issues.description: The manuscript states that Table 2 provides demographic and descriptive statistics, but the provided Table 2 contains only a title and note without the actual values. This prevents readers from evaluating sample composition, scale distributions, and comparability across studies.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study’s descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.description: The manuscript does not report how participants were recruited, whether they received course credit or compensation, response rates, consent context, or whether data collection occurred in classrooms, labs, or online participant systems. These details are needed to evaluate sampling bias and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US where the replications were conducted from February, 2016 to June, 2017

issues.description: The introduction frames hypotheses partly as Facebook compared with face-to-face interaction, but the Methods indicate that expression and connection items assessed whether Facebook enabled these outcomes, without explicitly saying they were comparative to face-to-face interactions. If expression and connection were not measured comparatively, conclusions about Facebook being better than FTF for those constructs are not supported.
issues.quote: Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others. Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF.

issues.description: Self-esteem and all Facebook-perception outcomes were self-reported in the same session, often under researcher-administered conditions. This creates shared method variance and possible demand effects, particularly because participants first completed self-esteem and then evaluated Facebook disclosure affordances.
issues.quote: After informed consent, participants completed the 10-item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale ... Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions

issues.subcategory: broad conclusion not limited to sampled population
issues.description: The conclusion generalizes to future researchers and low-self-esteem individuals broadly, without consistently limiting the inference to U.S. undergraduate Facebook users in 2016–2017. This overstates external validity.
issues.quote: future researchers can be relatively confident of finding that low self-esteem predicts perceptions that Facebook is a safer and more advantageous place to self-disclose than FTF interactions.
